rv.q: This is a 'Wizard of Oz' with all possible fantastical trappings. But after an evening in this headache-inducingly loud and bright fantasy, you may well be wishing you were home, along with Dorothy.
It all feels a bit hollow beneath the shiny exterior, like the Tin Man's chest cavity.
But it's also good, respectful fun.
Foster's production of this most enchanting of stories is efficient rather than inspired.
Steely, earnest and bold, her 'Over the Rainbow' is performed with skilful panache, with Onuorah imbuing the number with a deep-seated sense of desperate longing.

“Foster’s production is certainly a spectacle...Douglas O’Connell’s digital projections dominate, whirling up storms and giving us a bird’s-eye view of Kansas farmlands...I wondered if younger viewers could actually follow the narrative.
Few will feel shortchanged by a show that offers great songs, real spectacle and a sprinkling of starry talent.
It doesn't break new ground, but it is very family friendly and audience reaction marks it a crowd pleaser.
Like the characters, Foster's production is smart, brave and full of heart, it's pure joyous escapism, and for a musical like this, there really is no place like the London Palladium.

As Ado Annie she was the best thing in a dismal deconstructed Oklahoma! and here brings a feisty, pigeon-toed vulnerability to Dorothy from Kansas who lands in Oz. The warmth of her smile, and soaring vocals in Somewhere over the Rainbow will pierce your heart.

cn.t: Foster's high-octane revival dazzles with extravagant visuals and Onuorah's standout Dorothy, but critics are divided on its relentlessly busy, steampunk-infused approach—some find it exhilarating family fun, others exhausting spectacle over substance.
